query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Coating a conventional self‐lubricating high‐entropy alloy (HEA) with a nanoscale 2D high‐entropy alloy lubricant—in particular, a thin, uniform layer of a transition‐metal dichalcogenide high‐entropy compound (e.g. (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2)—will reduce both the coefficient of friction and the wear rate over a wide service-temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: A bulk HEA (e.g., a typical CoCrFeMnNi‐type alloy) with its standard microstructure and without any engineered surface lubrication features.
generation.intervention: Apply a nanoscale coating of 2D high‐entropy alloy lubricant (e.g. dispersion of (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2 nanoflakes) onto the HEA surface via a conventional air‐spray or similar deposition process that ensures uniform coverage and good adhesion.
generation.conditions: Ball‐on‐disk tribological tests under ambient and controlled atmospheres across a wide temperature range (from room temperature up to ~800 °C), at representative normal loads (e.g., 1–9 N) and sliding speeds, mimicking the operating conditions of self‑lubricating moving components.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an in situ tribocatalytically active, shearable nanocomposite surface layer where the 2D nanolubricant is aligned and intimately bonded to the substrate.
generation.mechanism: The 2D HEA lubricant coating provides a stable, low-shear interface that (1) physically separates contacting surfaces and (2), through its inherent tribochemical activity, forms a lubricious tribofilm during sliding. This dual action reduces interfacial shear stress, suppresses adhesive and abrasive wear, and maintains low friction even as temperature varies.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to an untreated HEA surface, the intervention is predicted to significantly lower the average coefficient of friction and reduce wear rates (potentially by one to two orders of magnitude) over the tested temperature range.
generation.baseline: An untreated HEA exhibiting higher friction coefficients and faster wear under the same loading and temperature conditions.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness is expected as long as the coating adheres robustly and remains intact under the mechanical loads and thermal cycling; performance may degrade if delamination or severe deformation of the coating occurs beyond the designed operating envelope.
generation.uncertainty: Precise numerical improvements and the durability of the coating under prolonged cyclic loading remain to be quantified; variations in coating uniformity and adhesion could also affect outcomes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one group of the standard HEA and another group with the 2D HEA lubricant coating applied via air spray deposition. Subject both sets to identical ball‐on‐disk sliding tests at several temperatures (e.g., RT, 400 °C, and 800 °C) and loads (e.g., 1–9 N) in a controlled atmosphere. Use profilometry, microscopy, and friction measurements to quantify the sliding friction coefficient and wear rate.
measurements: Average coefficient of friction over sliding cycles
Wear track depth and wear volume (via optical profilometry or equivalent)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant decrease in both the friction coefficient and wear rate (e.g., by at least an order-of-magnitude improvement compared to the untreated HEA) across the temperature range, or if the coating fails to remain intact during testing, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: To examine the longevity and performance of the HEA coating for extended durations, the long‐run endurance tests were performed till failure at different loads of 1N, 5N, and 9N. Interestingly, the experiments show that 2D HEA lubricant works better at higher loads (Figure 2d). The tests ran for sliding distances of 525, 1040, and 1590 m at 1, 5, and 9N, respectively, before failure. So far, the superior lubricious effect of 2D HEA could be demonstrated from the low friction and wear rates, also accompanied by its extended longevity, especially much better performance at high loads, which increases the interest in the friction mechanism of 2D HEA.

High hardness and good wear resistance have been revealed for the high-entropy alloy (HEA) system AlCoCrFeNiTi, confirming the potential for surface protection applications. Detailed studies to investigate the microstructure and phase formation have been carried out using different production routes. Powder metallurgical technologies allow for much higher flexibility in the customisation of materials compared to casting processes. Particularly, spark plasma sintering (SPS) enables the fast processing of the feedstock, the suppression of grain coarsening and the production of samples with a low porosity. Furthermore, solid lubricants can be incorporated for the improvement of wear resistance and the reduction of the coefficient of friction (COF). This study focuses on the production of AlCoCrFeNiTi composites comprising solid lubricants. Bulk materials with a MoS2 content of up to 15 wt % were produced. The wear resistance and COF were investigated in detail under sliding wear conditions in ball-on-disk tests at room temperature and elevated temperature.
